title: Tokenizer Toy — Byte-Pair Encoding, One Merge at a Time
description: A clearly labelled toy BPE tokenizer trained in your browser on a short original story or your own text. Step through merges one at a time with the ranked pair counts, watch merges and learned tokens pile up to a target vocabulary size, then tokenize any input as coloured chips with IDs, and see rare words shatter, digits split one by one, whitespace become tokens and accented letters fall to <unk>.
prompt: Build 'Tokenizer Toy': a clearly labelled toy byte-pair-encoding tokenizer trained in the page, on a small built-in corpus of original text or on text I paste. Let me step through merges one at a time with the pair frequencies, watch the vocabulary grow to a target size, then tokenize any input with coloured token boundaries and IDs. Show how rare words, numbers and whitespace split. Say plainly that it's illustrative and not any production model's tokenizer. Make it tactile, like letterpress blocks on kraft paper.

methodology: Algorithmic oracles computed from the corpus: the first merge (' ' + 't', seen 58 times, new ID 98), the ranking of candidate pairs, and the recount after a merge are asserted exactly.
A hand-checkable micro-corpus ('ab ab ab ab') proves merge order, stopping when no pair repeats, and encoding by merge rank ('ab ab abc' → ab | ·ab | ·ab | c).

Golden tokenization of a representative sentence after training to 200 tokens, token by token with IDs, plus property checks: the same string always maps to the same ID, and digits stay single when the corpus has no numbers.
Vocabulary accounting: 97 base characters plus <unk> gives 98, training stops exactly at the target, and lowering the target replays fewer merges.
Edge inputs: newline and tab tokens with visible markers, non-ASCII characters mapped to <unk> (ID 0) while their original text is kept on screen.
risks: Off-by-one vocabulary accounting (does <unk> count?); an early test caught exactly this, and the copy now states it.
Tie-breaking between pairs with equal counts must be deterministic, or merges and golden IDs would drift.
Encoding has to apply merges by rank, not by greedy longest match, or tokens differ from what training learned.
Very long custom corpora making each merge step slow, since every step recounts all pairs.
qa.playwright: Nothing here is random or time-based, so tests assert exact training results. The page exposes pair rows (data-a, data-b, data-count), merges (data-token, data-rank) and tokens (data-text, data-id), which evaluateAll turns into arrays compared with toEqual. The first run failed on the vocabulary size (98, not 97, because <unk> counts), which led to clearer copy rather than a weaker assertion. Range inputs are driven with fill(), and the custom corpus with fill() on the textarea, which also covers its localStorage persistence across reload.
coverage: First merge, pair ranking, recount after merge, ×10 stepping
Train to target, lower target, reset
Golden tokenization with IDs, rare word, digits, stable IDs, hide IDs
Newline/tab tokens and <unk> for accented characters
Custom corpus training, stop condition, rank-order encoding, persistence

a11y: All controls are native buttons, a range with an <output>, and labelled textareas. Merge results are announced in a polite live region, token chips carry their text and ID as visible text (IDs can be hidden), and whitespace is shown with explicit ·, ↵ and ⇥ symbols rather than colour alone.
